This page summarises the method. The derivation and its checks are in the
report of the project the package grew out of (to be published).

## Why this method

Areal models in space and time attach a latent value to every area-time
cell, but surveys usually reach only a small fraction of the cells. The
standard tools treat the empty cells in one of two ways. Each makes one of
two operations on a Gaussian vector cheap and the other expensive:

- **Marginalising**, integrating some cells out, is free when the model is
  specified by its covariance: the observed cells' covariance is just
  their rows and columns. This is how Gaussian-process (geostatistical)
  models work. They carry only the observed locations, and they predict
  the rest afterwards by kriging. **Conditioning**, the rest given the
  observed, then needs dense matrix solves.
- Areal priors (CAR, Leroux, BYM, AR1 and random walks in time) are
  usually specified by their **sparse precision** matrix, a Gaussian
  Markov random field (GMRF). Here conditioning is cheap, needing only
  sparse blocks of the precision. Marginalising destroys the sparsity: the
  precision of the observed cells alone is a dense Schur complement.
  GMRF-based software (INLA, Rue et al. 2009; CARBayes, Lee 2013; ICAR
  models in Stan, Morris et al. 2019) therefore keeps
  a latent value for every cell, empty or not, because that is what keeps
  the algebra sparse.

With hundreds of areas and a few decades of months, the full table holds
tens of thousands of cells. That is a heavy load for MCMC, and coarser
time steps are often chosen to keep it down. *stareal* takes the
Gaussian-process route for areal models. For a *separable* space-time
prior, the covariance between any two cells is the product of a small
spatial and a small temporal matrix. The observed cells' covariance is
therefore cheap, as for a Gaussian process, while the areal prior is kept.
The model is fitted on the observed cells alone, and the full surface is
rebuilt afterwards, one posterior draw at a time.

This pays off when the data are sparse relative to the space-time grid:
fine time steps, many areas, few surveys, as is typical of molecular
surveillance. It does not when most cells are observed, when the prior is
not separable (for example, temporal correlation that varies by area), or
when there are tens of thousands of areas.

## The model

Space is a set of $m$ areal units (districts, counties, grid cells) with an
adjacency graph; time is a regular grid of $T$ steps (months, quarters,
years). An *area-time cell* is one area in one time step. Surveys report
$y$ positives out of $k$ tested. For each observed cell,

$$
y_{at} \sim \text{Binomial}\big(k_{at},\ \text{logit}^{-1}(x_{at})\big), \qquad
x_{at} = z_{at}^\top \beta + f_{at} + \epsilon_{at}.
$$

- $z_{at}^\top \beta$ are the **fixed effects**: an intercept, by default a
  linear trend in time (`trend()`, from $-1$ at the first step to $1$ at
  the last), and any covariates, which may vary by area, by time or by both.
  Their prior is Gaussian, $\beta \sim N(b_0, B)$.
- $f$ is a **Gaussian field** with separable covariance
  $\Sigma = \Sigma_t \otimes \Sigma_s$:
  - in space, a prior on the adjacency graph, by default the Leroux
    conditional autoregressive model (the choices are in the next
    section);
  - in time, a first-order autoregression with unit variance and lag-one
    correlation $\rho_t$.
- $\epsilon_{at} \sim N(0, \sigma_n^2)$ is a **cell-level nugget**: variation
  between surveys that the smooth field does not explain. It applies to the
  observed cells; the predicted surface is the field without it.

**Surveys in the same cell are pooled** into one count, $y_{at}$ of
$k_{at}$. This rests on an assumption: given the cell's latent value
$x_{at}$ (nugget included), the surveys in it are independent binomial
samples of one prevalence. A sum of independent binomial counts with a
common probability is binomial, so under that assumption pooling loses
nothing. The model has no variation between surveys within a cell. Two
surveys of different sites in the same district and month are treated as
one larger survey. If they differ by more than binomial sampling, through
different sites, populations or methods, pooling overstates how much the
cell's data say. Longer time steps and larger areas put more surveys
together, and make this more likely.

The hyperparameters $\theta = (\sigma, \rho_s, \rho_t, \sigma_n)$ have
half-normal and Beta priors (`areal_priors()`). Any of them can be held at
a value instead (`fit_areal(fixed = )`), for example $\rho_t = 0$ for a
field with no memory from one time step to the next.

## Spatial priors

$W$ is the adjacency matrix of the graph, $D$ the diagonal matrix of each
area's number of neighbours, and $R = D - W$ the graph Laplacian. The
priors that `fit_areal(spatial = )` offers all share the parameters
$\sigma$ (the scale) and $\rho_s$ (the strength of spatial dependence).
In every one, $\rho_s = 0$ makes the areas independent:

| `spatial` | The field at one time step | $\rho_s$ |
|---|---|---|
| `"leroux"` (the default; Leroux et al. 2000) | precision $\sigma^{-2}\{\rho_s R + (1 - \rho_s) I\}$ | 0 to 1 |
| `"bym2"` (Riebler et al. 2016) | covariance $\sigma^2\{\rho_s R_\star^{+} + (1 - \rho_s) I\}$ | 0 to 1 |
| `"car"` (the proper CAR) | precision $\sigma^{-2}(D - \rho_s W)$ | 0 to below 1 |
| `"iid"` | the Leroux prior at $\rho_s = 0$: covariance $\sigma^2 I$ | fixed at 0 |
| `"icar"` (Besag et al. 1991) | the Leroux prior at $\rho_s = 1$: precision $\sigma^{-2} R$ | fixed at 1 |

- **Leroux** moves between independence and the intrinsic CAR (ICAR) with
  one parameter, and stays a proper prior for $\rho_s < 1$.
- **BYM2** is the Besag-York-Mollié model reparameterised: a mix of a
  scaled ICAR and independent noise. $R_\star^{+}$ is the generalised
  inverse of $R$, scaled so that the geometric mean of its diagonal is 1.
  $\sigma$ is then roughly the marginal standard deviation of the field,
  whatever the graph, and $\rho_s$ the share of its variance that is
  spatially structured. The name $\rho_s$ is shared with the other priors,
  but its meaning is not the same as in Leroux.
- **The proper CAR** shrinks each area towards $\rho_s$ times the mean of
  its neighbours. Its marginal variances differ between areas: they are
  larger where there are fewer neighbours.
- **ICAR** is improper: it says nothing about the field's mean over the
  areas. *stareal* gives that direction zero variance, so the field sums
  to zero over the areas at every time step. The regional level, and its
  changes over time, then come from the fixed effects alone: with the
  default formula, a linear trend.

BYM2 and ICAR need a connected graph (`areal_frame()`'s island links make
one), and the proper CAR needs every area to have a neighbour.

All five have the same form. The spatial covariance is
$\Sigma_s = V \operatorname{diag}(g) V^\top$, for a basis $V$ computed once
when the frame is built: the eigenvectors of $R$ for Leroux, BYM2, iid and
ICAR, and those of $D^{-1/2} W D^{-1/2}$, rescaled, for the proper CAR. Only
the vector $g$ depends on $\sigma$ and $\rho_s$. So every prior costs the
same to fit and to predict, and the rest of this page applies to each.

## Fitting on the observed cells only

Most area-time cells have no data: in the
[crt K76T tutorial](crt76t.html), 264 of 74,304 unit-months. Because everything except
the likelihood is Gaussian, the unobserved cells can be integrated out
*exactly*: the $n$ observed cells' latent values $x_o$ have the Gaussian
prior

$$
x_o \sim N\big(Z_o b_0,\ \Sigma_{oo}\big), \qquad
\Sigma_{oo} = \Sigma_t[t_o, t_o] \circ \Sigma_s[a_o, a_o] + Z_o B Z_o^\top + \sigma_n^2 I,
$$

where $a_o$ and $t_o$ are the observed cells' areas and time steps and
$\circ$ is the elementwise product. The fixed effects are integrated out
too (the $Z_o B Z_o^\top$ term) and drawn afterwards from their exact
conditional distribution. The spatial block $\Sigma_s[a_o, a_o]$ comes from
the basis of the previous section, computed once when the frame is built,
so a change of $\sigma$ or $\rho_s$ only rescales its eigenvalues.

The MCMC therefore works on $n$ latent values, not $m \times T$, and its cost
per iteration grows as $n^3$, independently of the size of the full table.
This is what makes continental maps over decades, at monthly resolution,
feasible.

## The sampler

Each iteration updates the latent values, then the hyperparameters.

- **Latent values** by elliptical slice sampling (Murray, Adams &
  MacKay, 2010) against a *posterior-scaled* Gaussian (Nishihara, Murray &
  Adams, 2014): the Gaussian prior combined with a Gaussian approximation of each
  cell's likelihood (pseudo-data), with the approximation divided back out,
  so the update is exact. Proposing on this ellipse, rather than the
  prior's, is what lets heavily surveyed cells mix.
- **Hyperparameters** by two adaptive Metropolis moves: a centred move
  ($\theta$ given $x_o$) and the surrogate-data move of Murray and
  Adams (2010), in which $x_o$ moves with $\theta$. The centred move alone gets
  stuck, because $n$ latent values pin $\theta$.
- **During burn-in** the proposals adapt, and the pseudo-data are refitted
  twice to a Gaussian approximation of the likelihood at the chain's mean
  latent values. Both are then fixed, so the draws after burn-in come from
  an exact MCMC. The refit matters most for rare outcomes, where many cells
  have no positives.
- **Chains** start from dispersed points and run in parallel; `diagnose()`
  checks R-hat and effective sample sizes of every parameter, the latent
  value of every observed cell included.

## Prediction and aggregation

For each posterior draw of $(\theta, \beta, x_o)$, the full $m \times T$
surface is drawn by conditional simulation (Matheron's rule): an
unconditional draw of the field, corrected by kriging so that it agrees
with $x_o$. This is exact, and needs no matrix larger than $n \times n$
beyond the stored eigenvectors; the work is split into blocks of areas so
that memory stays bounded.

Each draw of the surface is then aggregated to any grouping of the areas
(regions, countries) as a weighted mean, and only then summarised. Group
estimates therefore carry the correlation between their areas, which
averaging area-level summaries would lose. The groupings can be the
frame's, or new ones given to `predict()`. With `group_draws`, the draws of
the aggregates are returned too. Anything derived from them, such as the
change between two years or the difference between two regions, is then
computed draw by draw and keeps the joint uncertainty.

## Cross-validation

`crossval()` holds out folds of observed cells, refits, and predicts each
held-out cell from its exact conditional distribution given the fitted
cells, nugget included. The log predictive density integrates that
Gaussian against the binomial likelihood by adaptive Gauss-Hermite
quadrature, and calibration is checked with a randomised probability
integral transform.

## Leave-one-out from one fit

[`loo()`](../reference/loo.stareal_fit.html) approximates leave-one-out cross-validation, one observed cell at a
time, without refitting. Plain Pareto-smoothed importance sampling
(PSIS-LOO; Vehtari et al. 2017) reweights the posterior draws by
$1/p(y_i \mid x_i)$. Here that fails. Each observed cell has its own latent
value $x_i$, which its own surveys pin down, so a few draws dominate the
weights.

The remedy (Vehtari et al. 2016) is to integrate $x_i$ out first. Given the
hyperparameters and the other cells' latent values, $x_i$ is Gaussian. Its
mean and variance follow from the precision $P = \Sigma_{oo}^{-1}$ of the
observed cells:

$$
x_i \mid x_{-i}, \theta \sim N\!\left(x_i - \frac{\{P(x_o - \mu_o)\}_i}{P_{ii}},\ \frac{1}{P_{ii}}\right),
$$

where $\mu_o$ is the prior mean. One Cholesky factorisation per draw gives
this for every cell at once. The binomial likelihood is integrated over
that Gaussian by quadrature, as in `crossval()`. The result is the
predictive density of a new survey of cell $i$ given everything else.
PSIS then works on these densities, which vary much less from draw to
draw. On simulated data, the approximation agrees with exact leave-one-out
(one refit per cell) to well within its standard error.

`compare_models()` lines up several fits of the same data cell by cell.
It reports each model's expected log predictive density, its difference
from the best, the standard error of that difference, and the effective
number of parameters $p_\text{loo}$. It does not report AIC, BIC or DIC.
AIC needs a number of parameters, which a model with a latent value per
cell does not have. BIC approximates a marginal likelihood, which in a
hierarchical model is driven by the priors. And DIC is unreliable for
latent Gaussian models.

Leaving one cell out keeps its neighbours in, so [`loo()`](../reference/loo.stareal_fit.html) measures how well
a model fills the gaps between data. For extrapolation, to areas or
countries with no data, `crossval()` with folds by region is the test.

## Scale

Two things set the cost of a fit:

- **The eigendecomposition of the graph.** `areal_frame()` does it once.
  It is a dense $m \times m$ problem, costing $O(m^3)$ in the number of
  areas $m$: quick for hundreds of areas, noticeably slower for thousands.
  Build the frame once and save it with `saveRDS()`.
- **Each MCMC iteration.** It costs $O(n^3)$ in the number of observed
  cells $n$, because of a dense Cholesky factorisation. It does not depend
  on the number of areas or time steps.

The sampler is almost entirely dense linear algebra, so an optimised BLAS
(Intel MKL, OpenBLAS or Apple Accelerate) makes a large difference over
R's reference BLAS. The method was developed on about 1,300 and 1,800
observed cells. Prediction holds one block of areas at a time, so memory
stays bounded however many draws are used.
